subject: Engelska 6
title: Grammar: passive voice and reported speech
sourceSummary: Active and passive forms in different tenses, plus how to change direct speech into indirect speech (reported speech) with correct tense backshifting.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is in the passive voice?
questions.opener: Look for the form "be" + past participle — that's the tell-tale sign.
choices: The committee announced the results yesterday.
The results were announced by the committee yesterday.
The committee will announce the results soon.
The committee is announcing the results now.
questions.explanation: In the passive voice, the one affected by the action ("the results") becomes the subject, and the verb is "be" + past participle: "were announced". The other options have the subject performing the action, i.e. the active form.

questions.prompt: Rewrite in the passive: "Millions of people watch this show every week."
questions.opener: Who or what is affected by the action? That should become the subject of the new sentence.
choices: This show is watched by millions of people every week.
This show was watched by millions of people every week.
This show watches millions of people every week.
Millions of people are watched by this show every week.
questions.explanation: The object "this show" becomes the subject, and since the main clause is in the present tense, the passive form is "is watched". Option 4 swaps who performs and who is subjected to the action, which changes the meaning entirely.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form: "The results ___ yet." (announce)
questions.opener: Present perfect passive is formed with have/has been + past participle.
choices: haven't announced
haven't been announced
aren't announced
weren't been announced
questions.explanation: Present perfect passive: have/has (not) been + participle — "haven't been announced". "haven't announced" is missing "been" and becomes an active form with the wrong meaning (it requires an object).

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form: "A decision ___ by Friday." (make)
questions.opener: Future passive: will be + past participle.
choices: will make
is made
will be made
will have make
questions.explanation: Future passive is formed with "will be" + participle: "will be made". "will make" is an active form and requires an object (who makes the decision), which is missing here.

questions.prompt: Report this statement: "I am tired," she said.
questions.opener: The tense is often shifted one step back (backshift) when the reporting verb is in the past tense.
choices: She said she is tired.
She said she was tired.
She said I was tired.
She says she was tired.
questions.explanation: "am" is backshifted to "was", and "I" changes to "she" since she is talking about herself. Keeping the present tense ("is") or "I" are the most common mistakes in reported speech.

questions.prompt: Report this question: "Where do you live?" he asked.
questions.opener: In indirect questions, the word order becomes like an ordinary statement — no auxiliary-verb inversion and no question mark.
choices: He asked where do I live.
He asked where did I live.
He asked where I live.
He asked where I lived.
questions.explanation: Indirect questions drop the auxiliary verb "do/did" and take normal word order (subject before verb), and the tense is backshifted: "where I lived". "where do/did I live" incorrectly keeps the question word order.

questions.prompt: Find and correct the three errors: "The teacher told to us turn off our phones, and she said that we not must talk during the test."
questions.opener: Look at three things: the preposition after "told", the verb form after the object, and where "not" should go together with "must".
questions.answer: The teacher told us to turn off our phones, and she said that we must not talk during the test.
steps: "told to us" → "told us": the verb "tell" is followed directly by the object, without a preposition ("tell someone to do something").
"us turn off" → "us to turn off": a reported command requires the infinitive with "to" after the object.
"we not must talk" → "we must not talk": negative modal verbs are formed with "must not", never "not must".
Summary: reported commands are formed with tell/ask + object + infinitive with "to", e.g. "told us to turn off", "asked us not to talk".

questions.prompt: Summarize how to form the passive in different tenses.
questions.opener: The same pattern in every tense — only the auxiliary verb "be" changes.
questions.answer: Present simple: am/is/are + participle — "The letter is sent." · Past simple: was/were + participle — "The letter was sent." · Present perfect: have/has been + participle — "The letter has been sent." · Future: will be + participle — "The letter will be sent." · Modal: modal + be + participle — "The letter must be sent." · Rule: only transitive verbs (verbs that take an object) can become passive, and "by + agent" is only added when it matters who performed the action.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly completes the passive transformation: "The chef prepared the meal." → "The meal ___ by the chef."
questions.opener: What tense was the active sentence in, and which participle form matches that in the passive?
choices: was prepared
is prepared
prepared
has prepare
questions.explanation: The active sentence is in the past simple ("prepared"), so the passive form is past simple passive: "was prepared". The other options have the wrong tense or an incorrect verb form.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form: "The bridge ___ in 1889." (build)
questions.opener: The date 1889 shows this is the past — which passive form goes with the past simple?
choices: was built
was build
has built
is building
questions.explanation: The date 1889 indicates the past, so the correct passive form is past simple passive: "was built". "was build" has the wrong participle, and the other options have the wrong tense or form.

questions.prompt: Report this statement: "We have finished the project," they said.
questions.opener: Present perfect in direct speech is backshifted to past perfect in reported speech.
choices: They said they had finished the project.
They said they have finished the project.
They said we have finished the project.
They said they finished the project since long.
questions.explanation: Present perfect ("have finished") is backshifted to past perfect ("had finished") in reported speech, and "we" changes to "they" since they are talking about themselves.

questions.prompt: Report this question: "Have you ever been to Paris?" she asked me.
questions.opener: Yes/no questions in reported speech begin with "if" or "whether", with normal word order.
choices: She asked me if I had ever been to Paris.
She asked me have I ever been to Paris.
She asked me if I have ever been to Paris.
She asked me if had I ever been to Paris.
questions.explanation: Yes/no reported questions begin with "if" or "whether" and take normal word order, with the tense backshifted: "if I had ever been". The other options incorrectly keep the question word order or the present tense.

questions.prompt: Report this command: "Don't touch that," the guide told the tourists.
questions.opener: Negative commands in reported speech: where does "not" go in relation to "to"?
choices: The guide told the tourists not to touch that.
The guide told the tourists to not touch that.
The guide told the tourists don't touch that.
The guide told to the tourists not touch that.
questions.explanation: Negative reported commands are formed with "not" + infinitive with "to": "told them not to touch". Placing "not" after "to" or omitting "to" is incorrect.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the passive correctly to emphasize the agent?
questions.opener: "by + agent" is added when it matters who performed the action.
choices: The novel was written by an unknown author in the 1800s.
The novel wrote by an unknown author.
An unknown author was written the novel.
The novel has write by an unknown author.
questions.explanation: "by + agent" is added after the passive form when it is relevant who performed the action: "was written by an unknown author". The other options have incorrect verb forms.

questions.prompt: Why might a writer choose the passive voice instead of the active voice in a sentence like "Mistakes were made"?
questions.opener: Think about what is missing from the sentence "Mistakes were made" compared with "I made mistakes".
choices: To avoid stating who is responsible for the action
Because passive voice is always grammatically required
Because the sentence has no verb in active form
Because passive voice is shorter than active voice
questions.explanation: The passive voice is often used precisely to avoid pointing out who is responsible for an action, as in "Mistakes were made", where no one is named as having made the mistakes. It is a stylistic choice, not a grammatical requirement.
